title: Advanced Computer Organization
blurb: CPU pipelines, hazards, cache hierarchy, coherence, branch prediction, virtual memory, and performance modeling with Python.
description: Connect CPU microarchitecture to measured software performance using Python simulations and calculations.

lessons.title: Pipeline fundamentals & CPI
lessons.explanation: A pipeline splits instruction execution into stages so different instructions can occupy different stages at the same time. Throughput can improve even though the latency of one instruction does not necessarily shrink.
examples:
instructions = 1200
cycles = 1560
cpi = cycles / instructions
print(f"CPI={cpi:.2f}")
commonMistakes: Confusing instruction latency with throughput or assuming a deeper pipeline always makes a single instruction finish faster.
lessons.explain: A pipeline splits instruction execution into stages so different instructions can occupy different stages at the same time. Throughput can improve even though the latency of one instruction does not necessarily shrink.

lessons.title: Data, control & structural hazards
lessons.explanation: Pipeline hazards are reasons the next instruction cannot advance safely. A RAW data hazard occurs when an instruction needs a result that an earlier instruction has not produced yet; forwarding can bypass that result directly to a later stage.
examples:
ops = [("LOAD", "R1"), ("ADD", "R1"), ("STORE", "R2")]
stalls = sum(1 for i in range(1, len(ops)) if ops[i-1][1] == ops[i][1])
print("estimated stalls:", stalls)
commonMistakes: Assuming forwarding removes every pipeline hazard.
lessons.explain: Pipeline hazards are reasons the next instruction cannot advance safely. A RAW data hazard occurs when an instruction needs a result that an earlier instruction has not produced yet; forwarding can bypass that result directly to a later stage.

lessons.title: Branch prediction & speculation
lessons.explanation: Branch prediction guesses the control-flow direction before the branch is fully resolved so the pipeline can keep fetching useful work. A branch target buffer can remember likely target addresses, while direction predictors learn whether a branch tends to be taken.
examples:
predicted = [True, True, False, True]
actual = [True, False, False, True]
correct = sum(p == a for p, a in zip(predicted, actual))
print("accuracy:", correct / len(actual))
lessons.explain: Branch prediction guesses the control-flow direction before the branch is fully resolved so the pipeline can keep fetching useful work. A branch target buffer can remember likely target addresses, while direction predictors learn whether a branch tends to be taken.

lessons.title: Cache hierarchy & locality
lessons.explanation: Caches exploit temporal locality, where recently used data is likely to be reused, and spatial locality, where nearby data is likely to be accessed soon. A cache hit is served from a faster level; a miss requires a slower level.
examples:
hit_time = 1
miss_rate = 0.08
miss_penalty = 80
amat = hit_time + miss_rate * miss_penalty
print("AMAT:", amat)
commonMistakes: Reasoning about cache size without the workload access pattern.
lessons.explain: Caches exploit temporal locality, where recently used data is likely to be reused, and spatial locality, where nearby data is likely to be accessed soon. A cache hit is served from a faster level; a miss requires a slower level.

lessons.title: Associativity, replacement & write policies
lessons.explanation: Associativity controls how many cache locations can hold a particular memory block, replacement policy decides which resident block is evicted, and write policy decides when modified data reaches the next memory level. Direct-mapped caches are simple but can suffer conflict misses; set-associative designs reduce those conflicts at extra hardware cost.
examples:
addresses = [0, 4, 8, 16, 0, 4]
line_size = 4
sets = 4
for address in addresses:
    block = address // line_size
    print(address, "set", block % sets)
commonMistakes: Treating associativity, replacement policy, and write policy as the same design choice.
lessons.explain: Associativity controls how many cache locations can hold a particular memory block, replacement policy decides which resident block is evicted, and write policy decides when modified data reaches the next memory level. Direct-mapped caches are simple but can suffer conflict misses; set-associative designs reduce those conflicts at extra hardware cost.

lessons.title: Virtual memory & TLB behavior
lessons.explanation: Virtual memory gives each process its own address space and maps virtual pages to physical frames through page tables. A TLB is a small cache of recent address translations.
examples:
address = 0x12345
page_size = 4096
page, offset = divmod(address, page_size)
print("page", page, "offset", offset)
commonMistakes: Treating a TLB miss as a page fault.
lessons.explain: Virtual memory gives each process its own address space and maps virtual pages to physical frames through page tables. A TLB is a small cache of recent address translations.

lessons.title: Multicore caches & coherence
lessons.explanation: Private per-core caches improve speed but create a consistency problem when multiple cores access data that maps to copies in different caches. Coherence protocols coordinate ownership and invalidation so writes become visible correctly.
commonMistakes: Confusing false sharing with a data race.
lessons.explain: Private per-core caches improve speed but create a consistency problem when multiple cores access data that maps to copies in different caches. Coherence protocols coordinate ownership and invalidation so writes become visible correctly.

lessons.title: Performance measurement & roofline thinking
lessons.explanation: Performance engineering begins with a reproducible workload and measurement. Hardware counters can reveal cache misses, branch misses, cycles, instructions, and other evidence.
examples:
import time
start = time.perf_counter()
value = sum(i * i for i in range(50000))
elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start
print(value, round(elapsed, 6))
commonMistakes: Trusting one noisy timing run or a benchmark that does not represent the real workload.
lessons.explain: Performance engineering begins with a reproducible workload and measurement. Hardware counters can reveal cache misses, branch misses, cycles, instructions, and other evidence.

exercises.title: Calculate CPI from a trace
exercises.prompt: Given 1,200 retired instructions and 1,560 cycles, calculate CPI. Then add 120 stall cycles and calculate the new CPI so you can explain exactly how stalls changed throughput.

exercises.title: Pipeline throughput vs latency
exercises.prompt: Model a five-stage pipeline processing a short instruction stream. Compare the latency of one instruction with the steady-state completion rate and explain why those are different measurements.

exercises.title: RAW hazard and forwarding
exercises.prompt: Given a short instruction dependency sequence, mark the RAW dependencies and calculate how many bubbles are required with no forwarding versus with forwarding.

exercises.title: Branch misprediction cost
exercises.prompt: Given branch frequency, predictor accuracy, and a misprediction penalty, calculate the expected cycles lost per instruction to branch mispredictions and explain which input most changes the result.

exercises.title: Average memory access time
exercises.prompt: Calculate AMAT from hit time, miss rate, and miss penalty. Compare two cache configurations and identify which one actually produces the lower expected access time.

exercises.title: Conflict misses vs associativity
exercises.prompt: Simulate a repeating address pattern in a direct-mapped cache and then a 2-way set-associative cache. Count hits/misses and explain which misses were reduced by associativity.

exercises.title: LRU replacement trace
exercises.prompt: For one cache set with limited ways, process an access sequence and show the LRU order after each access. Identify the exact block evicted when the set becomes full.

exercises.title: Write-back vs write-through traffic
exercises.prompt: For a sequence of reads and writes, count lower-memory writes under write-through and under write-back with dirty evictions. Explain the bandwidth and complexity trade-off.

exercises.title: TLB hit and miss behavior
exercises.prompt: Given a virtual-address access trace and a small TLB, count TLB hits/misses and distinguish a TLB miss that is resolved by a page-table walk from a true page fault.

exercises.title: False-sharing trace
exercises.prompt: Model two threads updating different variables that occupy the same cache line. Count the ownership/invalidation handoffs and explain why moving the variables to separate lines can improve performance without changing correctness.

exercises.title: Roofline bottleneck decision
exercises.prompt: Given operations performed, bytes moved, peak compute rate, and memory bandwidth, calculate arithmetic intensity and decide whether the workload is more likely compute-bound or memory-bandwidth-bound.

exercises.title: Benchmark locality change
exercises.prompt: Compare two access patterns over the same amount of data, run repeated timing trials, and explain whether the evidence is consistent with improved cache locality rather than assuming the first timing result is meaningful.

quiz.q: CPI stands for:
Pipeline throughput describes:
options: How frequently completed instructions/results can emerge once the pipeline is flowing
Only the latency of one instruction from start to finish

quiz.q: What does a pipeline stall normally do?
options: Adds cycles in which useful pipeline progress is delayed, increasing effective CPI

quiz.q: A RAW hazard occurs when:
options: A later instruction needs a value that an earlier instruction has not produced/written yet
Two cache lines have the same size
A branch is always predicted correctly

quiz.q: What is forwarding/bypassing used for?
options: Send a produced value directly to a dependent pipeline stage to avoid some waits
Write every cache line to memory immediately

quiz.q: What is a structural hazard?
options: Two pipeline operations need the same limited hardware resource at the same time

quiz.q: What happens after a branch misprediction in a speculative pipeline?
options: Incorrect speculative work is discarded/flushed and correct-path work must restart
The CPU gains extra cache capacity
The branch becomes a page fault

quiz.q: Why is predictor accuracy alone not enough to estimate performance cost?
options: You also need branch frequency and the penalty/cycles lost for each wrong prediction
Accuracy already includes every memory access
The predictor only affects disk I/O

quiz.q: A branch target buffer (BTB) helps predict/cache:
options: Where a taken branch should jump
Which thread owns a Python lock

quiz.q: Temporal locality means a program is likely to:
options: Access the same data/instruction again soon
Always access the next sequential address only

quiz.q: What is a cache hit?
options: The requested block is found in the relevant cache level
The CPU must always fetch from disk

quiz.q: A common AMAT model is:
options: hit time + miss rate × miss penalty

quiz.q: Increasing cache associativity mainly helps reduce:
options: Conflict misses caused by multiple blocks mapping to the same limited locations
Compulsory first-touch misses in every case

quiz.q: What does an LRU-style replacement policy try to evict?
options: The block that has not been used for the longest time among the candidates

quiz.q: How does write-back differ from write-through?
options: Write-back can defer lower-level memory updates until a dirty line is evicted, while write-through propagates writes immediately
Write-through never writes to lower memory

quiz.q: What does the TLB cache?
A TLB miss means:
options: The translation is not in the TLB and may require a page-table lookup
The page is definitely absent from physical memory
The cache line must be dirty

quiz.q: A true page fault occurs when:
options: The required virtual-memory page is not currently resident/valid for the access and OS handling is required

quiz.q: What is cache coherence for?
options: Keeping shared-memory views consistent enough across cores/caches according to the coherence model
Making every thread execute in order

quiz.q: What is false sharing?
options: Different threads modify different variables that occupy the same cache line, causing unnecessary coherence traffic
Two threads write the same variable without synchronization
A cache miss caused only by cold start

quiz.q: Why can contention reduce multicore speedup?
options: Multiple cores compete for shared locks, cache lines, bandwidth, or other resources instead of progressing independently
More cores always remove all bottlenecks
It increases memory bandwidth without limit

quiz.q: Why should a performance benchmark include repeated controlled measurements?
options: To distinguish a real effect from noise, warmup, and unrelated system variation
Because hardware counters work only on the second run
To guarantee every run has the same nanosecond time
To remove the need for representative workloads

quiz.q: In roofline reasoning, arithmetic intensity compares:
options: Amount of computation to bytes of data moved

quiz.q: Hardware performance counters can provide evidence about:
options: Events such as cache misses, branch behavior, instructions, and cycles depending on the CPU/tool
